title: Sales sold something that does not exist
summary: A closed deal depends on a feature nobody committed to. Four people need different messages and one of them signs the invoice.

brief.role: You are the PM for the integrations area.
brief.company: Stannis, a 250-person company selling HR software to mid-market employers.
brief.context: A deal closed last Friday worth $180k ARR. This morning you learned from the implementation team that the signed order form includes a line item for 'bi-directional payroll sync with Deltapay, available at go-live'. Go-live is in nine weeks. There is no Deltapay integration on your roadmap, none in development, and the account executive says he was told in a Slack thread three months ago that it was 'planned for the second half'. You have found that thread: an engineer said 'if we do Deltapay it'd probably be H2'. Your CTO's first reaction was 'that is not a commitment and I am not staffing it'.
brief.objective: Get to an outcome that keeps the customer, keeps the team's integrity, and does not repeat.
brief.constraints: Nine weeks to go-live. Your team of five is fully committed to a compliance deadline that cannot slip. The customer's HR director is the champion; the CFO signed.
brief.task: Decide what you do and how you communicate it, to whom, in what order.

evidenceCards.title: What was actually written down
evidenceCards.content:
The signed order form, section 3: 'Deltapay bi-directional payroll synchronisation, available at customer go-live.' It is one of eleven line items. Legal confirms it is a contractual deliverable, not a marketing statement.

The Slack thread, three months ago, in #sales-questions:
AE: 'Do we support Deltapay?'
Engineer: 'Not today. If we do Deltapay it'd probably be H2, it's on the long list.'
AE: '👍'

There is no other record. The order form was reviewed by legal for terms but there is no product sign-off step on order forms — anyone in sales can add a line item.

Two previous order forms in the last year contained feature line items that were not on the roadmap. Both were caught during implementation. Neither triggered a process change.

evidenceCards.title: What building it would take
evidenceCards.content:
From the integrations engineering lead:
'Deltapay has a public API. A one-way import of employee records is realistic — roughly three weeks for one engineer, and it covers the case where HR data flows from us into payroll.

Bi-directional sync is a different thing. Their API has no webhooks, so we would poll, and their rate limits mean a full reconcile for a 2,000-employee customer takes about forty minutes. Conflict resolution when both sides edit the same record is the hard part. Realistically eight to ten weeks with two engineers, and I would not want to ship the first version of it to a customer at go-live.

One more thing: the compliance work my team is doing has a regulatory deadline. If you pull anyone off it, we miss that, and that is a different kind of problem.'

evidenceCards.title: What the customer actually needs
evidenceCards.content:
The implementation manager called the HR director to understand the requirement before anyone panicked.

- The driver is that their payroll team currently rekeys new hires and salary changes from their old HR system into Deltapay, about 90 records a month, and it is error-prone.
- Asked what 'bi-directional' meant to her, she said: 'Honestly, the salesperson used that word. What we need is that when we hire someone or change a salary, it appears in payroll without anyone retyping it.'
- Payroll data flowing back into the HR system is described as 'nice, eventually' — the payroll team owns that data and does not currently expect it in the HR tool.
- The HR director is the champion and has staked internal credibility on this rollout. The CFO signed the contract and, per the AE, 'reads the order form line by line'.
- Go-live date is driven by their fiscal year start and is firm.

evidenceCards.title: Internal positions
evidenceCards.content:
CTO: 'A Slack message is not a commitment. I am not pulling people off compliance.'
VP Sales: 'The deal is closed and the number is in the quarter. Whatever we do, do not make it look like we are walking things back.' He has not yet been told the details.
Account executive: apologetic, and says he genuinely believed it was coming in H2. He is not a repeat offender.
Implementation manager: 'I can work with almost anything if I know what it is by next week. What I cannot do is find out in week seven.'
Your head of product: 'Your call. Tell me what you need from me.'

Company context: two similar surprises in the last year, no process change. The order-form template has no product review step.

decisionPrompt: What do you commit to, and how do you handle the people involved?

decisionOptions.label: Ship one-way sync for go-live and put bi-directional on a dated roadmap
decisionOptions.description: Build the three-week one-way import, take a written amendment to the customer covering what lands at go-live and when the rest follows, and fix the order-form process.
decisionOptions.consequence:
You call the HR director with the implementation manager, describe exactly what will work at go-live, and confirm it covers the rekeying problem. She is relieved rather than annoyed, because the thing she actually needs is covered.
The CFO requires a written contract amendment; legal produces one in a week specifying one-way at go-live and bi-directional within two quarters, with a service credit if missed. The CFO signs.
One engineer comes off compliance for three weeks; the lead reworks the plan and the regulatory deadline still holds with a week of slack.
A product review step is added to order forms the following month.
Trade-off: you committed the company to a dated follow-up you now have to fund, and you spent political capital getting a signed amendment rather than handling it informally.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale separates the customer's stated solution from their actual need, gets the change in writing because the CFO signed, sequences the internal conversations, and addresses the recurring process failure.

decisionOptions.label: Build bi-directional sync for go-live
decisionOptions.description: Honour the contract as written. Pull two engineers onto Deltapay for the nine weeks.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Two engineers move. The compliance deadline is missed by three weeks, which triggers a remediation plan with your regulator and consumes the legal team for a month.
Bi-directional sync is functionally complete at week nine and goes live with the customer as its first user. Conflict resolution fails twice in the first month on concurrent salary edits, producing two incorrect payroll records that the customer's team catches.
The HR director never needed the reverse direction. The AE learns that promising undeliverable things produces engineering effort rather than consequences.
Trade-off: you honoured the letter of a contract nobody wanted at the cost of a regulatory deadline and a shaky first release.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak. Nobody asked what the customer needed. It also treats an explicit regulatory deadline as tradeable and ships a first-version integration to a customer at go-live.

decisionOptions.label: Escalate internally and let leadership decide
decisionOptions.description: Take the conflict between the CTO's position and the VP Sales' position to your head of product and the exec team before talking to the customer.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The escalation takes eight days to resolve because the VP Sales is travelling. The exec team lands, predictably, on one-way at go-live with a written amendment — the same answer available in week one.
By the time the implementation manager is told, it is week three of nine. He absorbs it, but the amendment now has to be negotiated in five weeks rather than eight, and the CFO's office pushes back on the compressed timeline.
The customer conversation happens later and lands worse, because the champion had already told her CFO the feature was coming.
Trade-off: you got internal alignment before committing and paid for it with the two weeks that mattered most.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Some credit for not committing unilaterally. Mark down heavily for delaying the customer conversation when the implementation manager explicitly said he needs to know within a week.

decisionOptions.label: Remove the line item and offer a discount
decisionOptions.description: Tell the customer the feature was promised in error, take it out of the contract, and compensate with a price reduction.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The HR director is put in a difficult position: she championed this internally and now has to tell her CFO that a signed deliverable is being withdrawn. The CFO escalates to your VP Sales, who escalates to your CEO.
The deal survives with a 12% discount and a damaged relationship. Six weeks later the implementation team builds the one-way import anyway, because the customer's rekeying problem is real and blocking go-live.
You end up doing the work and paying the discount.
Trade-off: you were honest and fast, and you removed a capability the customer genuinely needed without checking first.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Credit the honesty. Low score because it skips the step that changes everything — asking the customer what they actually need — and gives away margin for a problem that had a three-week solution.

rubric.referenceReasoning: The trap is treating this as a contract dispute when it is a requirements problem. The customer's actual need — new hires and salary changes reaching payroll without rekeying — is one-way, three weeks, and does not touch the compliance deadline meaningfully. 'Bi-directional' was the salesperson's word, and the HR director says so herself. Once that is established, the question becomes how to make the change legitimate: because the CFO signed and reads line items, a verbal reassurance to the champion is not enough, so a written amendment is required. Sequencing matters as much as content. The implementation manager needs to know within a week, the champion needs to be equipped to explain this to her own CFO rather than ambushed by it, the VP Sales needs to hear it before the customer escalates to him, and the CTO's compliance deadline is a hard constraint, not a negotiating position. Finally, this is the third occurrence with no process change, so a strong answer fixes the order-form gap rather than only this instance.
evidenceSignals: Uses the HR director's own account that 'bi-directional' was the salesperson's word
Identifies that the real need is 90 rekeyed records a month, which one-way sync solves
Notes the CFO signed and reads line items, so the change must be in writing
Treats the compliance deadline as a regulatory constraint rather than a priority call
Notices this is the third such surprise and that no process change followed the first two
Notes the implementation manager needs an answer within a week

product_sense: Separates the contractual wording from the underlying job to be done
Recognises the reverse data flow has no owner on the customer side
analytics: Sizes the customer's actual problem (90 records a month) rather than reasoning from the feature name
user_research: Values the implementation manager's direct conversation with the champion over the AE's account
prioritization: Protects the regulatory deadline as non-negotiable
Chooses three weeks of work over eight to ten for the same customer outcome
execution: Gets the amendment in writing rather than relying on goodwill
Fixes the order-form review gap so the pattern stops
Gives the implementation manager an answer inside his stated window
communication: Sequences who is told what, in what order, and why
Equips the champion to defend the change to her own CFO rather than surprising her
Tells the VP Sales before the customer escalates to him
Avoids blaming the AE publicly while still closing the process gap

product_sense: Takes the contractual phrase 'bi-directional' as the requirement without checking it
prioritization: Treats the compliance deadline as something that can slip for a sales commitment
Commits eight to ten weeks of work when three achieves the customer's outcome
execution: Relies on a verbal reassurance when the signer reads line items
Leaves the order-form process unchanged after a third occurrence
communication: Delays the customer conversation while resolving an internal disagreement
Puts the champion in the position of discovering the gap from her own CFO
Makes the AE the story rather than the process

learnTakeaway.title: Check the requirement before you fight about the commitment
learnTakeaway.body: When a promise outruns the product, the instinct is to argue about who committed what. That argument is usually less useful than one phone call to the customer, because the words in the contract are frequently the salesperson's vocabulary rather than the buyer's requirement. Once you know the real job, the gap often shrinks from something you cannot deliver to something you can. Then the work is sequencing: get it in writing if the signer reads writing, and equip your champion before their finance team finds out on their own.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: The gap is smaller than the contract makes it look. The HR director told our implementation manager that 'bi-directional' was the salesperson's word — what she needs is hires and salary changes reaching payroll without rekeying, about 90 a month. That's the one-way import: three weeks, one engineer. Bi-directional is eight to ten and trades a $180k deal against a regulatory deadline. Order matters: VP Sales today, joint call with the HR director tomorrow so she can take it to her CFO herself, then a written amendment. This is the third order form like this; I want a product review step.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: I'd get internal alignment first, on a one-week clock. The CTO won't staff this and the VP Sales doesn't want it to look like we're walking anything back; those are irreconcilable as stated. If I call the customer and then get overruled, they see us contradict ourselves, which is worse than a week's delay. I also can't sign an amendment alone. Today I'd bring my head of product the one-way proposal with estimates and the HR director's own words, and ask for a decision by Friday. If I don't have one by then, I call the customer anyway and say so.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: It is in a signed contract and legal says it is a contractual deliverable, so we have to build it. The deal is worth $180k. I would pull two engineers onto Deltapay and talk to the CTO about the compliance work — maybe we can get an extension there.
